message.content:
Gerotranscendent Generativity: How Older Adults Maintain a Focus on “Being” for Others

Theresa Southam, MA, PhD Student; Fielding Graduate University

ABSTRACT

Generativity in older adults has predominantly been defined as tangible assets delivered to others, including caring for others, civic action, and community volunteerism (Hodgkin, 2012; De St Aubin & McAdams, 2004). Less light has been shone on non-physical contributions. In this research we learn how generative older adults focus on being rather than doing, while becoming what Edmondson (2015) calls socio-cultural message bearers, advisors on the human condition and creators of cultural and artistic products and practices.

RESEARCH GOALS, PARTICIPANTS AND METHODS

This ethnographic and phenomenologically informed research asked “What does it look like when older adults’ are contributing to the next generations from a gerotranscendent lens?”

Over two months, the researcher observed:

  • 14 participants in Intergenerational Leadership and Learning class co-facilitated by researcher.
  • Eight older adults recommended by a hospice society interlocutor who participated in two, 3-hour sessions: autobiographical life review (Wengraf, 2004) and life-cross roads (Kelsari & Palgi, 2017).
  • Three participants randomly selected from whole sample for phenomenological interviews.
[Diagram: Bubble network structure]
FIELDING
Graduate University

RESULTS

Records of group discussions, artwork, life crossroads diagrams, a survey and observations were coded as typifications – groupings based on shared experiences. A theme, raised independently by the participants during the group discussions and vigorously agreed on by all, is highlighted.

Typifications

Elders/Sages/Mentors: focus on just being by talking to people that no one will talk to, acting in a way that teaches and shows, communing with nature, “adopting” children that need soul grandparents, peer counseling and bringing spirit into the body.

Third Agers: focus on doing by being remembered for actions such as reinvigorating a community organization, advocating for more environmentally sound transportation, volunteering, and tutoring.

Overarching Theme

A focus on being rather than doing

“I feel sorry for people trying to save the world, I have a quieter more contemplative life at 70 then I had at 55.”

“The older I get, people look to me, I have so much gratitude.”

Autobiographical and Life’s Crossroads: Diagramming Life’s Coherence and Meaning

To the right, artwork and phrases that best represent the collective responses are provided. The survey is summarized in the chart.

Demographic of Eight Autobiographical and Life Crossroads Exercise Participants
Female Average Age Post Secondary Divorced Living Independently Spiritual Religious
6 69 4 3 All All None
[Image: Life Crossroads]
Figure 1: Participant Life Crossroads Diagram.
[Image: Boundaries]
Figure 2: Drawing of Observation of Boundaries between Self and Universe.
[Image: Gratitude]
Figure 3: Participant Drawing of Cultivating Gratitude and Heart.
[Image: Holding Light]
Figure 4: Holding Someone in the Light.
[Image: Community]
Figure 5: Community Support
Acknowledgements
This research was partly funded by a Social Transformation Grant from the Building Inclusive Collaborative of the Marie Fielder Center for Democracy, Leadership and Education at Fielding Graduate University
[Diagram: Bubble network structure]

CONCLUSIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Gerotranscendence described as where the boundaries between self and the universe dissolve.

Study participants agree on a shift in emphasis from age 55 where they were doing to 70 when they are being.

“People measure how much we give materialistically. They know there’s more and they feel compelled to share love.” Quote from research participant.

Next Steps

Although older adults are largely defined in contemporary EuroAmerican culture as a burden, they are in fact abundantly generative. The ability of older adults to continue learning, leading spiritual, artistic and contemplative lives, is supported by neurological studies (Cohen, 2005). Further research on the impact on the collective consciousness of older adults’ messages, advice and creations is warranted.

[Diagram: Bubble network structure]

REFERENCES

Erikson, M.C. (2010). Composing a further life: the age of active wisdom. New York, NY: Knopf.

Cohen, G.D. (2005). The mature mind: the positive power of the aging brain. New York, NY: Basic Books.

Edmondson, R. (2015). Ageing: insight and wisdom. Meaning and practice across the lifespan. Bristol, UK: Policy Press.

Erikson, E.H. & Erikson, J.M. (1998). The life cycle completed. Extended version. New York, NY: W. W. Norton.

Hodgkin, S. (2012). “I’m older and more interested in my community”: Older peoples’ contributions to social capital. Australian Journal on Ageing, 31(1), 34-39. doi:10.1111/j.1741-6612.2011.00528.x

Kelsari, S. & Palgi, Y. (2017). Life crossroads on stage: Integrating life review and drama therapy for older adults. Aging and Mental Health, Volume 21, Issue 10, 1079-1086.

Perry, R. (2014). Conscious aging: embrace and savour your next chapter. Simon & Schuster Inc.: New York, New York.

McAdams D & de St Aubin E. (1992). A theory of generativity and its assessment through self-report, behavioral acts, and narrative themes in autobiography. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 60 (1): 664-1252).

Rowe, J. & Kahn, R. (1998). Successful aging. New York, NY: Dell.

Tornstam, L. (2005). Gerotranscendence: A developmental theory of successful aging. New York, NY: Springer Publishing Company.

Wengraf, T. (2004). Qualitative research interviewing: Biographic narrative and semi-structured methods. Thousand Oaks, California: SAGE Publications Ltd.
